title: Sublime: Sublinear Error & Space for Unbounded Skewed Streams

statements.text: Like CS, provides unbiased estimates. Moreover, letting~$V(F)$ denote its estimation variance when using a size function~$W(·)$ and one array on a stream with squared~$ _2$ - norm $F = Σ_y (f(y))^2$, we have at the end of epoch~$i$ that $$ V(F_ i+1 ) ≤ 1 W_i · Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ i-j · (F_ j+1 - F_j), $$ where~$F_j$ denotes the squared~$ _2$ - norm of the stream at the start of epoch~$j$.

When using a sublinear power size as the function~$W(N)$, , has a memory footprint of~$≈ d · W(N) · [ 4.41 + 1.26 · log_2 N/W(N) ]$. With a linear size function, uses~$≈ d · W(N) · [4.41 + 1.26 · log_2(N log_2 N/W(N)) ]$ bits of memory. The same bounds hold for with~$W(F)$ instead of $W(N)$ and with an additive overhead of one bit per counter.

Letting~$E(N)$ denote the estimation error of when using a size function~$W(·)$ and one array on a stream with a total of~$N$ keys, we have at the end of epoch~$i$ that $$ E(N_ i+1 ) ≤ 1 W_i · Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ i-j · (N_ j+1 - N_j), $$ where~$N_ j $ for $j≥ 0$ denotes the total number of keys in the stream at the start of epoch~$j$.

Letting~$E(N)$ denote the error of when using a size function~$W(·)$ on a stream of total of~$N$ keys, we have at the end of epoch~$i$ that $$ E(N_i) ≤ Σ_ j=0 ^i N^ res (k) _j-N^ res (k) _ j-1 W(N_j)+1-k , $$ where~$N^ res (k) _j$ for $j≥ 0$ is the total count of the keys not among the top~$k$ at the end of epoch~$j$.

Letting~$E(N)$ denote the estimation error of when using a size function~$W(·)$ on a stream with a total of~$N$ keys, we have at the end of epoch $i$ that $$ E(N_i) ≤ Σ_ j=0 ^i N_j - N_ j-1 W(N_j)+1 ,$$ where~$N_ j $ for $j≥ 0$ denotes the total number of keys in the stream at the end of epoch~$j$.

Consider an FE sketch with only overestimation errors that processes growing streams with an error bound of~$E(N)$ and a confidence of~$1-δ$. Such a sketch must use at least~$N/E(N) · [Ω ( log 1/δ + loglog (N/E(N)) ) - Θ(1)]$ bits of memory at some point in time while processing a stream.

Consider a counter array of size~$w$ and let~$k$ be the sum of its counters' absolute values. When the counters are unsigned, \ encodes the array in~$w · [ 4.41 + 1.26 · log_2 (k/w) ]$ bits. When the counters are signed, it uses one extra bit per counter to encode their signs.

When working with unsigned counters and stubs of length~$s$ bits, \ encodes a counter value~$v$ in $s$ bits if $v < 2^s$ and in at most $4 + 1.26 · log_2 v$ bits otherwise. Signed counters use one more bit for encoding the sign in both cases.

We can fix the internal randomness of the FE sketch~$ S _ i^* $ such that, for at least half of the possible sequences~$ x $, i.e., $ u' ^n/2$ many of them, $μ( x ) ≤ 64δ/log_2 n$ and $ ( x ) ≤ 64δ/log_2 n$.
For any constant~$α<1$, it holds that $$ Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ j/α - 2^ (j-1)/α 2^ j = O(1) · 2^ i/α 2^i . $$
$$ Σ_ j=0 ^i N^ res (k) _j- N^ res (k) _ j-1 W(N_j)+1-k ≤ 4· E'_i. $$

proofs.text: If~$v < 2^s$, it fits in its stub and occupies~$s$ bits. Otherwise, its~$s$ lower-order bits are stored in its stub and its higher-order bits encoding~$ v/2^s $ are stored in an extension. This extension has~$ log_3 v/2^s + 2$ fragments to represent the digits and the delimiter. Thus, it occupies $$ 2 · ( log_3 v/2^s + 2) ≤ 2 · (log_3 2 · log_2 v/2^s + 2) ≤ 4 - s + 1.26 · log_2 v $$ bits. This, added to the~$s$ bits of space consumed by the stub, yields the result.

Applying lemma:single_counter_space to every counter within the array and summing results in a total memory footprint of~$m ≤ Σ_i max(s, 4+1.26 · log_2 |v_i|)$ bits. To simplify this expression, we bound the stub length~$s$ based on the total absolute counter values. Recalling 's tuning mechanics from sec:accommodating_skew , \ uses stubs that are slightly longer than the length of the average counter. In fact, it never sets~$s$ to be more than~2 bits longer than the average counter length. Formally, this corresponds to~$s ≤ 2 + 1 w · Σ_i log_2 |v_i|$, where~$v_i$ denote the signed value of the~$i$ - th counter in the array. Since the logarithm is a concave function, we use Jensen's inequality~ [cite] to bound the sum on the right-hand side as~$log_2(Σ_i |v_i|/w)$. Noting that the absolute counter values~$|v_i|$ sum to~$k$ yields $s ≤ 2+log_2(k/w) = 4 + log_2(k/(4w))$. Plugging into the memory bound from before yields~$m ≤ Σ_i 4 + max(log_2 (k/(4w)), 1.26 · log_2 |v_i|)$. We further bound each individual max term by max & ( 1.26 · log_2 k 4w , 1.26 · log_2|v_i| ) \\ & ≤ 1.26 · max ( log_2 k 4w , log_2|v_i| ) \\ & ≤ 1.26 · log_2 ( k 4w + |v_i| ), $$ max ( 1.26 · log_2 k 4w , 1.26 · log_2|v_i| ) ≤ 1.26 · max ( log_2 k 4w , log_2|v_i| ) ≤ 1.26 · log_2 ( k 4w + |v_i| ), $$ thus implying~$m ≤ Σ_i 4 + 1.26 · log(k/(4w) + |v_i|)$. Rearranging the sum and once again using the concavity of the logarithm to apply Jensen's inequality yields the desired result: m &≤ w · [4 + 1.26 · 1 w · Σ_i log_2(k/(4w)+k/w) ] \\ & ≤ w · [ 4.41 + 1.26 · log_2 (k/w) ]. $$ m ≤ w · [4 + 1.26 · 1 w · Σ_i log_2(k/(4w)+k/w) ] ≤ w · [ 4.41 + 1.26 · log_2 (k/w) ]. $$ -8pt

By a similar analysis to that of thm:cms-w , the sum of the absolute counter values within each array in \ when using a sublinear power as the size function is~$≈ N$, modulo a small constant factor. This constant factor become especially negligible in the space bound, since it will appear within a logarithm. Similarly, when the size function is linear, we have~$k ≈ N log N$. Plugging these values into the bound of~ thm:counter_array_per_counter_space and multiplying by~$d$ proves the result.

During epoch~$i$, we have at most~$N_ i+1 -N_ i $ fresh insertions (i.e., that have not been cancelled out by deletions). Let~$f_i(x)$ denote the increase, if any, in the frequency of~$x$ during epoch $i$. We observe that $Σ_x f_j(x) = N_ j+1 -N_j$ for all $j≥ 0$. This implies that, in our previous notation, $E(N_ i+1 ) ≤ I $, which can be expressed as $$ E(N_ i+1 ) ≤ I =Σ_ j=0 ^i Σ_x C _ j, I (x) · f_j(x). $$ In other words, the counter~$ I $ gets the frequency~$f_j(x)$ added to it if and only if the event~$ C _ j, I (x)$ occurs. We also have that~$ C _ j, I (x) = 2^ i-j /W_i$. By linearity of expectation, we then get I &= Σ_ j=0 ^i Σ_x 2^ i-j W_i · f_j(x) = 1 W_i · Σ_ j=0 ^i Σ_x 2^ i-j · f_j(x)\\ &= 1 W_i · Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ i-j Σ_x f_j(x) = 1 W_i · Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ i-j · (N_ j+1 - N_j). The claim follows.

‌\\ The Linear Case of~$W(N)=N/ε$. In this case, the size function doubles whenever the number of elements doubles, i.e., $N_ j+1 = 2 · N_j$ for all $j≥ 0$ and, in general, $N_j = 2^j · N_0$ for all $j≥ 0$. The additional error term then becomes: Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ i-j · (N_ j+1 - N_j) & = Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ i-j · (2^ j+1 · N_0 - 2^ j · N_0)\\ &= Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ i-j · 2^j · N_0 = (i+1) · 2^i · N_0\\ &= (i+1) · N_i\;. Plugging in this bound in the formula from lemma:cms-w (i.e., dividing by~$W(N_i)=N_i/ε$), we get the main claim for $W(N)=N/ε$. The Sublinear Case of~$W(N)=N^ α /ε$. In this case, the size function doubles more slowly, i.e., whenever~$N_ i+1 = 2^ 1/α · N_i$. Since~$0 ≤ α < 1$, $N_ i+1 $ is bigger than~$2· N_i$. This difference is why we do not have the extra dependency on~$i$ in the error term. Formally, we have that~$N_i = 2^ i/α · N_0$ and thus Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ i-j · (N_ j+1 - & N_j) = Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ i-j · (2^ (j+1)/α · N_0 - 2^ j/α · N_0)\\ &= Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ i-j · 2^ j/α · N_0 · (2^ 1/α -1) \\ &= 2^i · N_0 · (2^ 1/α -1) · Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ j/α- j \\ &= 2^ (1-1/α) · (i+1) - 1 · N_ i+1 · (2^ 1/α -1) · Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ j/α- j , where in the last step we have used~$N_0 = 2^ (-1/α)·(i+1) · N_ i+1 $. Simplifying the sum of the geometric series on the right as~$ 2^ (1/α-1)·(i+1) -1 2^ 1/α-1 -1 $ then yields Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ i-j & · (N_ j+1 - N_j) \\ &= 2^ (1-1/α) · (i+1) - 1 · N_ i+1 · (2^ 1/α -1) · 2^ (1/α-1) · (i+1) - 1 2^ 1/α-1 - 1 \\ &= N_ i+1 · (2^ 1/α -1) · 2^ -1 - 2^ (1-1/α) · (i+1) - 1 2^ 1/α-1 - 1 \\ &= N_ i+1 · (2^ 1/α -1) · 1 - 2^ (1-1/α) · (i+1) 2^ 1/α - 2 \\ &= N_ i+1 · (2^ 1/α -1) · 1 - 2^ (α-1) · log_2 (N_ i+1 /N_0) 2^ 1/α - 2 \\ &≤ N_ i+1 · 2^ 1/α -1 2^ 1/α - 2 . In the penultimate line, we have used the property that~$i+1$ is equal to $log_ 2^ 1/α (N_ i+1 /N_0) = log_ 2^ 1/α 2 · log_2 (N_ i+1 /N_0) = α · log_2 (N_ i+1 /N_0)$. Moreover, in the last line, we have removed the negative exponential to derive the final upper bound. The claim follows by plugging this bound in the expected error from lemma:cms-w .

We are interested in describing the behavior of the random variable~$ f (z) = I · σ(z)$ for any query~$z$, where~$σ(z)$ is $z$'s update direction and~$ I $ is the counter that~$z$ hashes into. Using the notation we introduced in sec:upper_bounds_cms , this counter~$ I $ can be expressed as: $$ I = Σ_ j=0 ^i Σ_x C _ j, I (x) · f_j(x) · σ(x) = Σ_x C (x), $$ where~$ C (x) = Σ_ j=0 ^i C _ j, I (x) · f_j(x) · σ(x)$ denotes the contribution of~$x$'s updates to counter~$ I $ throughout the epochs. We apply a similar analysis to that of a traditional CS to compute the expected value of the estimate~$ f (z)$, showing that~$ I · σ(z)$ is an unbiased estimator of~$f(z)$, i.e., $ I · σ(z) = f(z)$. In the following, we denote by~$f_j(x)$ the frequency of key~$x$ within epoch~$j$. By linearity of expectation, it holds that $$ f (z) = Σ_ x ≠ z C (x) · σ(z) + C (z)σ(z) = Σ_ j=0 ^i f_j(z) = f(z),$$ where the last step uses the property that~$ σ(x) · σ(z) = 0$ for any $x ≠ z$, in conjunction with~$ C _ j, I (z)=1$ since $h(z)= I $. This proves the first part of the lemma. We now turn to bound the variance of this estimator. In particular, we are interested in how much bigger it becomes compared to~$F_i/W_i$. Writing the definition of the variance, we get that f (z) &= Σ_x C (x) σ(z) ^2 - (f(z))^2 \\ & = Σ_x C (x) ^2 + Σ_x Σ_ y ≠ x C (x) C (y) - (f(z))^2 \\ & = Σ_x C (x) ^2 - (f(z))^2. In the third line we have used the property that~$ σ(x) · σ(y) =0$ for any $x≠ y$ to simplify~$ C (x) C (y) $ to 0. To bound~$ C (x) ^2 $, recall that we defined~$ C (x) = Σ_ j=0 ^i C _ j, I (x) · f_j(x) · σ(x)$. Then: C (x) ^2 &= Σ_ j=0 ^i C _ j, I (x) · f_j(x) ^2 \\ & = Σ_ j=0 ^i C _ j, I (x) · f_j(x) ^2 \\ & \;\; + 2· Σ_ j=0 ^ i-1 Σ_ k=j+1 ^i C _ j, I (x) · f_j(x) · C _ k, I (x) · f_k(x) \\ & = Σ_ j=0 ^i (f_j(x))^2 · C _ j, I (x) \\ & \;\; + 2· Σ_ j=0 ^ i-1 Σ_ k=j+1 ^i f_j(x) · f_k(x) · C _ j, I (x) · C _ k, I (x) . Here, we have used the property~$( C _ j, I (x))^2 = C _ j, I (x)$ (which follows from~$ C _ j, I (x)$ being an indicator random variable) to simplify the second line. To bound~$ C _ j, I (x) $, we use the definition of the epochs to conclude that~$ C _ j, I (x) ≤ 2^ i-j /W_i$. For $ C _ j, I (x) · C _ k, I (x) $, we note that the product of the two indicator random variables is $1$ only when both of them are $1$. Yet, the two random variables are not independent: if $ C _ k, I (x) =1$, then $ C _ j, I (x)=1$ for any $k≥ j$. Namely, if during epoch $k$, $x$ hashed into a counter …

We start with the original FE sketch~$ S _0$, which is used to process the stream until its squared~$ _2$ - norm reaches at most some~$F_0$. The Linear Case of~$W(F)=F/ε$. In this case, the size function doubles whenever the squared~$ _2$ - norm doubles, i.e., $F_ j+1 = 2 · F_j$ for all $j≥ 0$ and, in general, $F_j = 2^j · F_0$ for all $j≥ 0$. We therefore get that V(F) &≤ Σ_ j=0 ^ i F_ j+1 - F_j · 2^ i-j W_i \\ & ≤ 1 W_i · F_0 · 2^ i + Σ_ j=1 ^ i 2^ j+1 - 2^j · F_0 · 2^ i-j \\ & ≤ 1 W_i · F_0 · 2^ i + Σ_ j=1 ^ i 2^j · F_0 · 2^ i-j \\ & ≤ 1 W_i · F_0 · 2^ i + Σ_ j=1 ^ i F_0 · 2^i \\ & ≤ (i+1) · F_i W_i . The Sublinear Case of~$W(F)=F^ α /ε$. In this case, the size function doubles more slowly, i.e., whenever~$F_ i+1 = 2^ 1/α · F_i$. Since~$0 ≤ α < 1$, $F_ i+1 $ is bigger than~$2F_i$. Plugging this into the statement of~ lemma:cs-w , we have that~$F_i = 2^ i/(1-α) · F_0$ and thus 1 W_i · Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ i-j · & (F_ j+1 - F_j) \\ & = 1 W_i · Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ i-j · 2^ (j+1)/(1-α) · F_0 - 2^ j/(1-α) · F_0 \\ & = 1 W_i · Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ i-j · 2^ j/(1-α) · F_0 · 2^ 1/(1-α) -1 \\ & = 1 W_i · 2^i · F_0 · 2^ 1/(1-α) -1 · Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ j/(1-α) - j \\ & = O(F_ i+1 /W_i).

We begin by first defining some notation. Let~$C_i$ denote the sum of the counter stored in the sketch at the end of epoch~$i$ (with $C_ -1 =0$). Note that $C_i ≥ 0$, since we only decrement counters when they are all nonzero. We also denote by~$d_i$ the total number of keys that decrement the sketch's counts during epoch~$i$. By design, the following relationship holds for each~$i≥ 1$: $$ C_i = C_ i-1 + N_i - N_ i-1 - d_i · (W(N_i)+1). $$ To see why this is true, consider the case in which~$i=1$. At the beginning of the first epoch, the counts stored in the sketch add up to~$C_0$. During the epoch, we see~$N_1-N_0$ fresh insertions, each of which either increases the total count of the sketch by~1, or decrements~$W(N_1)$ counts. The number of keys among these~$N_1-N_0$ that make such decrements is exactly~$d_1$. In other words, there are~$N_1-N_0-d_1$ keys that increase the sketch counts by~1, and $d_1$ keys that decrease the sketch count by~$W(N_1)$. The total changes are therefore~$N_1-N_0-d_1 - d_1 · W(N_1)$, which is how we get the first expression. It follows from the general expression that $$ d_i = N_i - N_ i-1 + C_i - C_ i-1 W(N_i)+1 . $$ Now, for any specific key~$x$, the maximum error that we can make in its count is if we decrement its count every time we a key decrements the sketch's counts (i.e., this worst-case is achieved when the sketch stores all occurences of~$x$ from the beginning and then keeps decrementing one from its count every time it seems an unstored key). Formally, if we are at the end of epoch~$i$, then the error is bounded as $$ E(N_i) ≤ f(x) - f (x) ≤ Σ_ j=0 ^i d_j.$$ Plugging in our expression for~$d_j$ and using $W_j=W(N_j)$ for ease of notation yields Σ_ j=0 ^i d_j & = Σ_ j=0 ^i N_j - N_ j-1 + C_ j-1 -C_j W_j+1 \\ &= Σ_ j=0 ^i N_j - N_ j-1 W_j+1 + Σ_ j=0 ^i C_ j-1 -C_j W_j+1 \\ &=Σ_ j=0 ^i N_j - N_ j-1 W_j+1 + Σ_ j=0 ^ i-1 C_j · - 1 W_j+1 + 1 W_ j+1 +1 - C_i W_j+1 \\ &=Σ_ j=0 ^i N_j - N_ j-1 W_j+1 - Σ_ j=0 ^ i-1 C_j · W_ j+1 - W_j (W_j+1)(W_ j+1 +1) - C_i W_i+1 \\ &≤ Σ_ j=0 ^i N_j - N_ j-1 W_j+1 \;, where the last inequality holds because~$W_ j+1 >W_j$, so we are ignoring negative factors in the sum.

‌\\ The Linear Case of~$W(N)=N/ε$. In this case, we use the fact that in we increase the counters one by one as opposed to doubling them. In other words, we consider divisions into epochs for which~$W(N_ i+1 )=W(N_i)+1$ and hence $N_ i+1 =N_i+ε$. Plugging this into~ lemma:mg-w , we get at the end of epoch~$i$ that E(N_i)&≤ Σ_ j=0 ^i N_j - N_ j-1 W(N_j)+1 = N_0 W(N_0) + Σ_ j=1 ^i ε W(N_0)+j \\ &= ε + ε · Σ_ j=1 ^i 1 W(N_0)+j ≤ ε + ε · _ W(N_0)+1 ^ W(N_0)+i 1 x \,dx\\ & ≤ ε + ε · ln W(N_0)+i W(N_0)+1 ≤ ε · (1+ln i) ≤ ε · ln N. Here, the last line follows from~$i$ being the number of times we expand by one counter until we reach a stream length of~$N$, implying that~$i ≤ N/ε+1$. The Sublinear Case of~$W(N)=N^ α /ε$. In this case, it is easier to think of divisions into time in which we double the number of counters instead of increasing them one by one. That is, we define the epochs such that~$W(N_ i+1 ) = 2· W(N_i)$ and hence $N_ i+1 = 2^ 1/α · N_i$. Noting that~ lemma:mg-w holds irrespective of the specific definition of the epochs then yields Σ_ j=0 ^i N_j - N_ j-1 W(N_j)+1 & = Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ j/α · N_0 - 2^ (j-1)/α · N_0 2^j · W(N_0) \\ & = Σ_ j=0 ^i 2^ j/α - 2^ (j-1)/α 2^j · N_0 W(N_0) . Finally, by applying Claim~ [ref] , we get Σ_ j=0 ^i N_j - N_ j-1 W(N_j)+1 & ≤ O(1) · 2^ i/α 2^i · N_0 W(N_0) = O(1) · N_i W(N_i) . proving the desired result.

We start similarly as in the proof of~ lemma:mg-w and get that, if $d_i$ is the number of deletions to the sketch that occur during some epoch $i ≥ 0$, then it holds that $$ C_i = C_ i-1 + N_i - N_ i-1 - d_i · (W(N_i)+1). $$ Here, $C_i$ denotes the sum of the sketch's at the end of epoch~$i$ (with $C_ -1 =0$). We generalize the above to $$ C_i - C_ i-1 ≥ N^ (k) _i - N^ (k) _ i-1 - d_i · k,$$ where~$N^ (k) _i $ denotes total count of the top~$k$ keys at the end of epoch~$i$ (the top $k$ with respect to the whole stream). In other words, the change in the sketch counts is at least the change in the sketch counts restricted to the top~$k$ keys. This is because the total count restriced to these~$k$ keys increases by~$N^ (k) _i - N^ (k) _ i-1 $ and each of these~$k$ keys gets its counter decremented at most~$d_i$ times. Combining the equation and the inequality above and rearranging, we get that $$ d_i ≤ N_i - N_ i-1 -N^ (k) _i + N^ (k) _ i-1 W(N_i)+1-k = N^ res (k) _i- N^ res (k) _ i-1 W(N_i)+1-k . $$ Summing these terms proves the desired result.

Note that the additive terms in the bounds of thm:mg-res come from the application of thm:mg-normal to the portion of the stream that must be ``waited out'' by to create the~$k$ - th counter for the first time. We therefore focus on deriving the remaining part of the error bound, which corresponds to the error resulting from processing the stream with an instance of initialized with at least~$k$ counters. The Linear Case of~$W(N)=N/ε$. In this case, $W(N_ i+1 )=W(N_i)+1$ and $N_ i+1 =N_i + ε$. We consider an epoch~$i$ and define a series of integers~$i_ $ as follows. We start by defining~$i_1$ as the largest integer such that $$ Σ_ j=1 ^ i_1 N^ res (k) _j- N^ res (k) _ j-1 ≤ ε. $$ In words, we group consecutive terms of the form~$N^ res (k) _j- N^ res (k) _ j-1 $ until we are about to reach~$ε$. Note that $$ Σ_ j=1 ^ i_1+1 N^ res (k) _j- N^ res (k) _ j-1 ≥ ε, $$ as the maximality of~$i_1$ implies that the extra term~$N^ res (k) _ i_1+1 - N^ res (k) _ i_1 $ causes the sum to grow beyond~$ε$. We also define~$i_2 > i_1$ in a similar fashion as the largest index such that $$ Σ_ j=i_1+1 ^ i_2 N^ res (k) _j - N^ res (k) _ j-1 ≤ ε. $$ Like before, we stop right before we gather a sum of~$ε$. Moreover, as before, including the extra term~$N_ i_2+1 ^ res (k) -N_ i_2 ^ res (k) $ yields $$ Σ_ j=i_ 1 +1 ^ i_2+1 N^ res (k) _j- N^ res (k) _ j-1 ≥ ε. $$ We continue as such for~$ $ steps until we have that: $$ Σ_ j=i_ +1 ^ i N^ res (k) _j- N^ res (k) _ j-1 ≤ ε. $$ We now define~$i_0=0$ and upper bound~$ $ as N^ res (k) _i & ≥ Σ_ j=1 ^ i_ N^ res (k) _j- N^ res (k) _ j-1 \\ &≥ 1 2 · Σ_ s=0 ^ Σ_ j=i_ s +1 ^ i_ s+1 +1 N^ res (k) _j- N^ res (k) _ j-1 \\ &≥ 1 2 · Σ_ s=0 ^ ε = ε · /2, i.e., $ ≤ 2 N^ res (k) _i/ε$. Now we also observe that for every~$0 ≤ s ≤ $ it holds that Σ_ j=i_s+1 ^ i_ s+1 N^ res (k) _j- N^ res (k) _ j-1 W(N_j)+1-k &≤ Σ_ j=i_s+1 ^ i_ s+1 N^ res (k) _j- N^ res (k) _ j-1 W(N_0)+s+1-k \\ & ≤ ε W(N_0)+s+1-k . This is because~$W(N_j)+1-k = W(N_0)+j+1-k ≥ W(N_0)+s+1-k$, since $j ≥ i_s+1$ by the bounds of the summation and~$i_s+1 ≥ s$ by the way we parametrize the~$i_s$ while defining them. Putting everything together yields Σ_ j=0 ^i N^ res (k) _j- N^ res (k) _ j-1 W(N_j)+1-k &≤ N^ res (k) _0 W(N_0)+1-k + Σ_ s=0 ^ ε W(N_0)+s+1-k \\ & ≤ ε + ε · Σ_ s=0 ^ 1 W(N_0)+s+1-k \\ & ≤ ε + ε · _ W(N_0)+1-k ^ W(N_0)+ +1-k 1 x dx \\ & ≤ ε + ε · ln ≤ 2 ε + ε · ln N^ res (k) _i. Our proof follows a contradiction argument similar to the proof of Theorem~3.1 in~ [cite] . That is, we consider an FE sketch~$ S $ that, given a key~$x$, computes an estimate~$ f (x)$ such that $| E [ f (x)] - f(x)| ≤ E(N)$ and $ Var ( f (x)) ≤ V(N) = δ · (E(N))^2$. Note that, by Chebyshev's inequality, this FE sketch guarantees an estimation error of~$2E(N)$ with a confidence of~$1-δ$.
